final_script.audience: General public with secondary-school science literacy

beats.narration: Your gut is home to trillions of bacteria, and there's a popular idea that transplanting them from a lean animal into another one could make it leaner too. A mouse experiment put that idea to the test — and the answer is more complicated than the headline.
beats.on_screen: Title card: 'Can gut bacteria make you lean?' Simple animation of gut microbes moving from one mouse to another.

beats.narration: Researchers used germ-free mice — mice raised with no gut bacteria of their own — and colonised them with microbes from either a lean donor or an obese donor. Eight weeks later, the lean-donor group had gained twenty-four percent less fat. Twenty mice per group, and statistically significant.
beats.on_screen: Two mouse groups side by side; bar chart showing -24% fat mass; caption 'p = 0.003, n = 20 per group'.

beats.narration: Here's the catch. That number comes from just one pair of donors. The team actually tested four, and the results were all over the place: minus six percent, plus three percent, minus nineteen percent. Only two of the four showed a clear effect.
beats.on_screen: Four bars appear: -24%, -6%, +3%, -19%, with p-values. The first bar is highlighted, then the other three fade in.

beats.narration: Put all four together and the average effect shrinks to about eleven percent, with a margin of error wide enough to include no effect at all.
beats.on_screen: Pooled estimate -11% with error bar spanning -23% to +1%, crossing a marked zero line.

beats.narration: And there's a bigger twist. When the researchers fed both groups exactly the same amount of food, the difference almost vanished — four percent, not statistically significant. So much of the original effect wasn't the bacteria at all. It was how much the mice ate.
beats.on_screen: Food bowls equalised between the two groups; the -24% bar collapses to -4% labelled 'not significant'.

beats.narration: The authors are clear: the effect depends on which donor you pick, and it largely fades once eating is controlled. It's a reminder that a striking headline figure can rest on one slice of a study — and the supplementary material is often where the real story lives.
beats.on_screen: Text on screen: 'Donor-dependent. Attenuated when food intake is controlled.' Then: 'Check the supplementary data.'

final_narration:
Your gut is home to trillions of bacteria, and there's a popular idea that transplanting them from a lean animal into another one could make it leaner too. A mouse experiment put that idea to the test — and the answer is more complicated than the headline.
Researchers used germ-free mice — mice raised with no gut bacteria of their own — and colonised them with microbes from either a lean donor or an obese donor. Eight weeks later, the lean-donor group had gained twenty-four percent less fat. Twenty mice per group, and statistically significant.
Here's the catch. That number comes from just one pair of donors. The team actually tested four, and the results were all over the place: minus six percent, plus three percent, minus nineteen percent. Only two of the four showed a clear effect.
Put all four together and the average effect shrinks to about eleven percent, with a margin of error wide enough to include no effect at all.
And there's a bigger twist. When the researchers fed both groups exactly the same amount of food, the difference almost vanished — four percent, not statistically significant. So much of the original effect wasn't the bacteria at all. It was how much the mice ate.
The authors are clear: the effect depends on which donor you pick, and it largely fades once eating is controlled. It's a reminder that a striking headline figure can rest on one slice of a study — and the supplementary material is often where the real story lives.
